title: Woodrail: a cozy woodblock train sim
author: DatabaseNearby5
selftext:
**What it is**

Almost a month ago I had a dream that I was vibe coding a Brio-style automation game. When I woke up I thought: did that really happen? Should it?

This is the end result. It's far from perfect, but I have a good time playing it :)

https://i.redd.it/9z3cc3gw690i1.jpeg

https://i.redd.it/t7jt1fhx690i1.jpeg

https://i.redd.it/zex7figz690i1.jpeg

https://i.redd.it/2md78uzz690i1.gif

**How the work is split**

I'm a software developer with 15+ years of experience (RIP my career, only half joking), but this game was entirely vibe-coded, with heavy guidance/direction from me. The stack isn't too far outside the norm for this sub (three.js + Blender + Claude Code), so I'll focus on my development process and how it changed along the way.

Right now the project is over 186k lines of TypeScript and 2,500+ commits (up to 250 in a day), so it's gotten a little bit out of hand.

I started with a pretty lengthy planning session before anything was built. I wanted to get the direction, gameplay and general vibe clear to Claude as early as possible. After that I had Claude mock up a couple of assets to nail down the style.

Once I had a working prototype, I started a parallel track where I told Claude to "take inspiration from Brio sets, but don't copy anything directly" and build as many game assets as it could. It took about 12 hours, running overnight, and I ended up with over 100 assets (it's now closer to 500). There's no AI image generation anywhere: every model is code, either a Blender Python script or a small TypeScript kit of toy parts. This was mostly for fun, but it also helped me think up features to add to the game later.

More specifics on my setup. I'm using:

* Claude Code in the Mac desktop app, plus the Claude mobile app (the first couple of days of dev were done almost entirely on mobile). That was more to get a feel for it than anything else, since I use the terminal CLI a lot at work. My impression: you have a tiny bit less control, but there are some nice quality-of-life things.
* Opus 5.5 on the "Ultra" plan. You could do something like this on a cheaper plan, but my career depends on staying on top of AI stuff, so a low-risk project I enjoy working on is worth the cost for me.
* Agent setup:
   * One "chief of staff" agent that orchestrates everything. It's told to delegate aggressively to subagents (up to 10 in parallel) and to make sure adequate "manual" testing is done for anything non-trivial.
   * The chief of staff also keeps a couple of Claude artifacts up to date. "Woodrail work board" shows the status of all the development work, plus any open questions that need my attention. "Woodrail Bigger Ideas" is where we hash out anything that needs a more detailed plan. Recently I wanted more to work towards in the late game, so we iterated there on a plan for some larger "grand projects" for players to build.
   * Mostly cloud agents do the development, but I keep one local session running in case I need computer control for anything (mainly loading web pages). The `/remote-control` command in Claude Code lets you chat with local sessions from your phone, and it works quite well!

**What worked**

* Real end-to-end "manual" testing. Claude was cheating on the tests at the start, and in the original version of the game you couldn't get past the first couple of milestones. I changed the structure so tests have to play the game the way a player would, and now QA catches quite a few bugs.
* Actual manual playtesting is so important. Even if things work in theory, they can be broken in practice. Rail placement, for instance: it was really hard to make tracks actually line up after twisting and turning around the map, and not the fun kind of hard. I ended up (1) letting the rails shift a bit and give some slack as you place them (kind of like real blocks), (2) adding an "auto" straight piece that fits into gaps more flexibly, and (3) adding a "draw" tool so you can just doodle track onto the play area (standard pieces are still there for the purists). There are still some quirks, but it's 100x better than where we started.
* Automated performance checks are great for catching perf problems before a deploy.
* itch.io has been a great place to put a browser game: a free page, an active community, and its own analytics.

**What went wrong**

* I had a long-running QA session looping very quickly on a 900k+ token context window. That almost single-handedly got me to my usage limit three days into the week. My lesson: big-context sessions aren't so bad when you're just chatting, but if they're looping they can and will murder your usage. After that I switched to spawning a fresh QA agent for each feature, and things have been a lot better.
* The game crashed for my first playtester who wasn't me. It looks like the phone ran out of GPU memory and dropped the WebGL context on a Pixel 10 (somehow a Pixel 7 was fine). The game now cuts its memory use and recovers when that happens.

**Conclusion**

So yeah, that's the journey of Woodrail. Very curious if anyone has any thoughts or feedback. Happy to go into more details if folks are curious about anything!

**Try it**

If you want to try it: [https://dwfennell.itch.io/woodrail?ref=r-aigamedev](https://dwfennell.itch.io/woodrail?ref=r-aigamedev) (free, in the browser, no signup).
